alignments.note: Expressed copula εἰσίν → 'Are'. The supplied subject pronoun goes to the expressed Greek subject πάντες, not here: rule 9 licenses a subject on a finite verb, but this clause expresses its subject, and the chapter puts the subject word on the expressed token throughout (1:5 αὐτός → 'he' beside ἔσται → 'shall be', 1:11 σύ → 'thou' beside διαμένεις, 1:12 σύ → 'thou' beside εἶ → 'art'). The inversion that writes 'Are they' together is English word order, which rules 53 and 63 refuse as a licence.
Rule 64: οὐχί carries content of its own and is aligned in the ordinary way, as 'not'; it is not a bare question marker for rule 44 to empty.

Substantival quantifier subject → 'they … all', the supplied pronoun a rule 7 helper on it exactly as at 1:11's 'they all', discontinuous around 'not' under rule 15 and headed on 'all'. Corrected from the accepted reading, which gave 'they' to εἰσίν. The competing reading is the corpus's εἰμί → 'are they', but those six units stand in clauses expressing no subject, whereas πάντες is the expressed masculine nominative subject here. Rule 87 does not join the quantifier to οὐχί: the ASV writes two English words, which rule 87's closing clause leaves to the ordinary split.
Attributive adjective rendered 'ministering', split from its noun under rule 26.
Predicate noun, anarthrous and given no determiner.
Participle rendered 'sent forth', the particle belonging to the English verb rather than to the preposition, which stands elsewhere in the clause.

Purpose εἰς realized by the word introducing its English clause, the infinitival 'to', under rules 36 and 40. Rule 61's bare-infinitive clause is not the case here, since a preposition is expressed for the 'to' to answer to; leaving εἰς unrepresented and giving 'to do service' whole to the noun is the competing reading, and rule 36 refuses it because English does realize the preposition.

The supplied 'do' is an empty support verb selected by the noun — you 'do' service as you 'bear' witness and 'give' thanks — so rule 7 gives it to the word that licenses it and rule 91's support-verb clause makes it a helper on the meaning-bearing complement, headed on 'service' under rule 17. Rule 62 is not the case: it is scoped to a verbless Greek clause whose prepositional phrase is the predicate, and this clause expresses εἰσίν while εἰς διακονίαν modifies ἀποστελλόμενα.

Rule 67's complex frame 'for the sake of', carried whole by the expressed preposition. Rule 67 leaves the head open for a proper preposition, and the prepositional word is taken on rule 46's stated test — the identical English heads on 'sake' or 'cause' only for the postposition χάριν, and on the prepositional word wherever a Greek preposition is expressed — which is also how rule 78 settles the discontinuous 'for … sake' wrap. A head on 'sake' is the competing reading and stands in the corpus for a contiguous frame on a proper preposition elsewhere.

Rule 32: a substantival article before a participle supplies the pronoun and nothing else, so it takes 'them' alone and the relativizer stays with the participle. Rule 90 is not in question, the ASV writing two English words for the pair.

μέλλω is realized by the futurity auxiliary 'shall', and the supplied relativizer 'that' is its rule 7 helper under rule 32. Headed on 'shall' because that is the word realizing this lexeme, not on the relativizer; rule 17's preference for a lexical verb over an auxiliary does not reach inside a unit whose only lexical realization is the auxiliary.
Complementary infinitive; the English infinitival marker is absorbed into the 'shall' periphrasis, so the verb stands on its own word.

review_notes: One edge moved: t002 'they' from εἰσίν to πάντες. εἰσίν keeps 'Are' and its head; πάντες keeps its head on 'all'. All 13 source ids and all 20 target ids remain partitioned exactly once.

The competing reading is the corpus's εἰμί → 'are they' (2CO.11.22 twice and four others, headed on 'are'). It does not carry here: those clauses express no subject, so the pronoun has nothing but the verb to belong to, whereas πάντες is the expressed masculine nominative subject of this clause and πνεύματα the neuter predicate.
The discontinuity is between 'they' and 'all' only; 'not' stays with οὐχί and no intervening word is absorbed.
Rule 87 is still not in question: the ASV writes the negation and the quantification as two separate English words, which rule 87's closing clause leaves to the ordinary split.

The rest of the verse is left exactly as the verse pass returned it, including 'do' on διακονίαν rather than on εἰς, and the head of διά → 'for the sake of' on 'for' with 'sake' named as the competing reading.
